title: engineer-trial-pair-notes-aurora-zhou
content:
Candidate: Luca Moretti (applied for Senior Inference Runtime Engineer)
Session type: 75m pair-program + 15m async debrief (me + Aidan)
Format notes: open laptop pairing on a small kernel-selection + batching stub; we asked them to design an API for a generic request router that can select model variant based on latency budget and cost tier, then implement a simplified batching loop with backpressure.

High-level impression: solid systems-first engineer. Comfortable reasoning about throughput/latency tradeoffs and memory usage. Clear about KV caching tradeoffs and eager vs lazy eviction. Code style is pragmatic but sometimes leans to one-off solutions rather than composable abstractions — fine for product teams but flag if we need library-level thought. Communicates well; asks clarifying Qs early.

What they did well:
- Quickly sketched routing API: Request {model_id, budget_ms, cost_tier} -> candidate variants; included fallback chain + prefetched kv-cache keys. Good call to include per-request telemetry hooks.
- Batching implementation: used async queue + timer-triggered flush; handled max-batch-size and max-wait-ms. Showed awareness of head-of-line blocking and suggested a priority queue by latency budget.
- Memory reasoning: estimated KV cache footprint and proposed working-set-sized cache + LRU; argued for per-tenant cache partitioning to avoid noisy neighbor.
- Deployment/operational awareness: proposed a canary rollout path that pins model variants and a circuit-breaker to fall back to smaller models under OOM/latency spikes.

Weaknesses / concerns:
- Implementation detail: their async flushing relied on a single global mutex around the batch vector; they acknowledged it as a simplification but did not propose sharding or lock-free options until prompted. For our high-throughput targets, this needs more concrete plan.
- Quantization/compute kernels: knows conceptually about int8 and q4xx quantization and the implications for accuracy, but limited hands-on experience converting models or running per-layer profiling. Not a showstopper but reduce expectation for immediate quantization leads.
- Language bias: prefers Go for runtime services; little recent C++/CUDA experience. Could be fine if role leans into Go orchestration layers, but if we need low-level kernel work they'd be ramping.

Scorecard (1-5):
- System design & architecture: 4
- Algorithms / batching & caching: 4
- Low-level performance / kernels: 3
- Code quality & maintainability: 3
- Communication & collaboration: 5
- Production ops / SLO thinking: 4

Concrete examples from the session:
- On backpressure: recommended fast-path when queue length > threshold -> direct route to smaller model; good quick recovery strategy.
- On cold-start caching: suggested saving lightweight index of recent prefixes so warm-up can be prioritized; nice practical touch.
- On the mutex: their initial code held the mutex while awaiting async network call — we flagged that and they rewrote to copy the batch vector out under lock then release before I/O. Shows they can iterate.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups for take-home or next-round:
- Can they propose a sharded batching approach (per-core or per-tenant) that keeps latency SLOs while achieving high utilization? Ask for a short diagram and complexity analysis.
- Request a short write-up describing how they'd instrument kernel selection (what metrics, sampling rate, how to detect regressions) — useful to judge readiness for Optimize work.
- Explore whether they'd be comfortable owning a C++/CUDA PR with mentorship — ask for recent contributions or open-source pointers.

Recommended next step: move to a focused architecture review (hooks: SRE + runtime kernel SME). Not urgent on deep kernel ownership; strong fit for a role that sits between serving orchestration and performance tuning. Recommend: onsite loop with one systems-design block + one whiteboard around sharded batching and a short take-home on instrumentation (2–4 pages).

Hiring rubric comment (for panel):
- Likely strong IC3/IC4 depending on ramp for low-level kernels. Excellent at cross-team tradeoffs and owning end-to-end feature.
- Risk: time to ship kernel-level perf wins if that is the primary job.

Action items (meera):
- Share these notes to #hiring-runtime and tag Aidan/Samir for quick thumbs (today).
- Send Luca the follow-up ask: 2-day take-home prompt + request for any OSS links. Draft message: "Thanks for pairing — we'd like a short design write-up on sharded batching and a brief note on kernel instrumentation; 48–72h window is fine."
- If panel thumbs are positive, schedule onsite with SRE + runtime-kernel SME (Samir to coordinate availability next week).

Personal reflection: enjoyed the session — candidate balances practicality with good instincts about production tradeoffs. If we hire them, they would accelerate system-level product work and be a solid mentor for newer engineers on the team.

Raw snippets I want to copy into the panel packet:
- "Prioritizes latency budget per request and will fall back to cheaper model variants automatically; includes telemetry hooks for each fallback"
- "Iterates quickly on an implementation when given feedback (replacing blocking mutex with copy-on-write for batch dispatch)"

Links & refs used during pairing:
- small toy repo we used: github.com/redwood-inference/interview-exercises/batching-stub (branch: pair-session-luca)
- related Jira for batching infra: ENG-1187

End of notes.
